month of the same search rarely changes it.

{middle_paragraph}

Every candidate is pre-vetted and trained on firm work before you meet
them. Interviewing costs nothing, and someone who fits can start in under
three days.

If it would help, I'll send two profiles matched to that seat. No
obligation either way.

templates.subject: {tort} intake, and the records volume behind it
templates.body:
Hi {first_name},

I saw that you're running {tort} intake.

On a docket like that the bottleneck is rarely signing claimants. It's the
four to six provider requests behind every one of them, all against a
filing deadline. None of that time is billable, and it's usually the first
thing to break when the volume arrives.

We staff exactly that work with document collectors who do nothing else
and are trained before they reach you. Free to interview, and able to
start in under three days.

Worth a short conversation before the volume lands?

arriving faster than anyone can return them, and the signed case going to

days.

templates.used_when: Every hourly firm (tier 4), whatever the pain
templates.subject: The hours nobody at your firm can bill
templates.body:
Hi {first_name},

This is a narrower note than the one you usually get from people like me.

I'm not going to suggest a paralegal. Yours are billable, and moving
billable work off your own books would be a poor trade for you.

It's the rest that interests me: the bookkeeping, the intake calls, the
marketing admin. Nobody bills for those and they still take someone's day.
That's the part we'd staff, with someone trained for it, pre-vetted, and
free to interview.

Worth ten minutes to see whether the numbers work?

steps.title: The arithmetic
steps.purpose: Why those hours cost this firm money, in the terms of how it bills.
steps.varies_by: Chosen by the fee model. Never a general version.

templates.subject: The unbilled hours between you and the fee
templates.body:
Hi {first_name},

A different angle on the same thing.

On contingency, every hour your team spends chasing records is unbilled,
and it sits between you and the fee. A demand writer isn't a saving. It
shortens the gap to settlement, which is a different argument entirely,
and the reason personal injury firms are usually the easiest version of
this conversation.

If it's worth ten minutes, I'll walk you through how those numbers tend to
look at a firm your size.

templates.subject: Who actually pays for those hours
templates.body:
Hi {first_name},

A different angle on the same thing.

The defendant pays the fees. Your own labour getting there's still an
unbilled input — records, employer files, agency forms — and nobody
reimburses the time it took to chase them.

It's the same arithmetic as contingency, and noticeably fewer people are
having this conversation with you.

Ten minutes to go through the numbers?

templates.body:
Hi {first_name},

On a flat fee the price is fixed the day you're retained. Every extra hour
on that matter comes straight out of the margin on that specific matter,
which makes this unusually easy to measure: you'll see the effect on the
next twenty cases, not next year.

Worth ten minutes to run those numbers together?

steps.title: A comparable firm
steps.purpose: A firm of the same shape that started the same way.

templates.subject: A firm about your size, the same problem
templates.body:
Hi {first_name},

A six-attorney personal injury firm we work with had the same shape of
problem: advertising was bringing in cases faster than two paralegals
could process them, and the backlog was in the records.

They started with one demand writer. Within a couple of months their
paralegals had stopped doing records entirely and gone back to case work,
which is what they were hired for.

I'm not saying that's you, but the pattern is common enough to be worth
mentioning.

templates.subject: Confidentiality, supervision, and how this actually works
templates.body:
Hi {first_name},

The question I'm usually asked around now is about client information, so
let me answer it before you have to ask.

Your person works inside {cms} under permissions you set, exactly as an
in-house hire would. They're HIPAA-trained, and the NDA and
confidentiality agreement are signed before day one. You supervise the
work the way you'd supervise anyone's, and you can end the arrangement at
any point.

I'm happy to send the agreement over to read before we ever speak.

steps.title: A second seat
steps.purpose: A different, smaller role, in case the first was the wrong one.

templates.subject: I may have aimed at the wrong end of this
templates.body:
Hi {first_name},

It's possible I've been writing about the wrong half of the problem.

If the bottleneck isn't the demand side but the front of the file —
requests going out, chasing providers, the clinic that never responds —
then what you need is a document collector rather than anything larger.
It's a smaller commitment and a faster thing to try.

Which end hurts more? I'll send profiles for that one instead.

steps.title: The other person
steps.purpose: Offers to talk to the office manager instead.

templates.subject: Am I writing to the right person?
templates.body:
Hi {first_name},

I may be writing to the wrong person entirely, which would explain the
silence.

If someone else at the firm handles hiring and case workflow — an office
manager or a firm administrator — I'm glad to talk to them instead and
leave you out of it. A name is all I need.

Otherwise I'll take it that the timing isn't right, and leave you in
peace.

tracks.label: Sequence
tracks.description: Up to nine emails, Day 1 to Day 29. An email with nothing true to say to a firm is left out, never padded.

tracks.label: Nurture
tracks.description: Emails 1, 3 and 9 at half the pace: Day 1, Day 15 and Day 57. With no pain on record the first is left out.

tracks.label: Strike
tracks.description: Written by hand, the same day. A need nobody else has seen is worth a person's own words, so the engine drafts nothing.
